title: KAP: Bridging the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption Gap in LLM Systems
event_hint: QiYuanLab paper (arXiv:2607.24260v1, 2026-07-27) proposes Knowledge Access Planning (KAP), a serving-time IR that compiles structured knowledge priors into physical KV-access policies, instantiated as the GraphSpec compiler-executor on vLLM.
problem: Knowledge-augmented LLM systems (RAG, GraphRAG, HippoRAG) produce rich structured priors (ranked evidence, graph topology, confidence), but prompt serialization collapses these into a flat token stream, forcing the serving backend to densely consume the full key-value (KV) state during decoding. The authors name this the Knowledge Selection-Runtime Consumption (KSRC) gap: richer contexts enlarge the KV footprint and decode-time memory traffic, raising latency and hurting throughput even when reasoning depends on a small fraction of the context.
mechanism: KAP elevates structured knowledge priors from prompt-construction hints into first-class physical execution artifacts via a universal intermediate representation-the runtime access plan-that compiles knowledge signals to govern physical KV access without altering logical prompt semantics, model weights, or training. It is instantiated as GraphSpec: a compiler-executor pairing a Graph-RAG knowledge-selection frontend with a vLLM serving backend, producing a selected-KV proposal view with full-context verification. A phase-boundary cost model characterizes the positive-speedup regime via the margin h-s between proposal acceptance rate (h) and retained-KV ratio (s).

evidence.claim: GraphSpec reduces proposal-visible KV access from 40.1% of source KV at 4K down to 5.5% at 128K, with decode throughput (TPS) speedup rising from 1.08x to 1.19x over full-context vLLM as context grows.
evidence.condition: GraphSpec TPS 48.80 at 128K; long-context QA workload, 4K-128K; Graph-RAG priors frozen pre-benchmark; frontend retrieval excluded from TTFT

evidence.claim: Answer quality is preserved: pass-rate difference vs full-context is at most 0.3 percentage points at five of six lengths, and 1.9 points higher at 64K (87.9% vs 86.0%); average similarity stays closely matched (e.g., 0.748 vs 0.741 at 64K).
evidence.value: GraphSpec pass 87.9% vs 86.0% full-context at 64K; <=0.3pp gap elsewhere
evidence.baseline: Full-context decoding (same LLM-as-judge similarity metric, 0.5 threshold)
evidence.condition: 4K-128K context sweep; pass rate = fraction with weighted LLM similarity >= 0.5

evidence.claim: The runtime access plan, not evidence selection alone, drives the gain: materializing the same selected evidence as a 0.95K-token prompt (Physical concat) drops pass rate to 73.9% vs 87.9% for GraphSpec at 64K, while Random concat and Local window fall to 49.7% and 47.1%.
evidence.value: Physical concat 73.9% vs GraphSpec 87.9% pass at 64K
evidence.baseline: GraphSpec (full logical prompt preserved) vs Physical/Random/Local concat on vLLM
evidence.condition: 64K contexts; GraphSpec accessed KV/source 10.8%, TPS 51.70 vs full-context 45.68

evidence.claim: Empirical speedup tracks the phase-boundary prediction: retained ratio s falls from 0.401 to 0.055 across 4K-128K while acceptance h stays high (~0.95+), so the margin h-s rises from 0.557 to 0.897 alongside measured speedup rising 1.08x to 1.19x.
evidence.baseline: Phase-boundary cost model (directional implication, not refit to measurements)
evidence.condition: 4K-128K contexts; h = Top-3 tolerant proposal acceptance rate

evidence.claim: The LLM-as-judge pass criterion was independently audited: on 100 SPIQA samples, thresholded judge decisions agreed with majority-vote human labels on 95%; evidence recalls were answer 68.8%, rationale 66.8%, caption 76.8%.
evidence.baseline: Three independent human annotators, blinded to LLM scores, majority vote
evidence.condition: 0.5 threshold fixed before audit; token-level/ROUGE-1 coverage of gold evidence

evaluation_context: Long-context QA workloads swept 4K-128K tokens. Backend: vLLM for full-context and concat baselines vs the GraphSpec executor. Graph-RAG evidence/priors frozen before benchmarking so frontend retrieval is excluded from TTFT; TTFT measured from frozen-request submission to first token and for GraphSpec includes runtime-access-plan compilation and selected-KV materialization; throughput covers the full executor path (not isolated model-forward). Quality via LLM-as-judge similarity in [0,1] with pass threshold 0.5 (fact consistency 40%, info completeness 30%, logical structure 20%, expression 10%). Audit dataset SPIQA.
limitations: Validates KAP through a single concrete instantiation (Graph-RAG frontend + vLLM backend); does not exhaust the broader design space. Results are strongest for long-context QA where graph-derived priors can be grounded in evidence spans and realized as backend runtime objects; effectiveness depends on prior quality, the compiler's translation, and backend execution without excessive metadata/scheduling/synchronization overhead. Gains are decode-throughput-only: GraphSpec TTFT is slightly higher than full-context at most lengths (e.g., 0.87s vs 0.65s at 8K, 1.56s vs 1.51s at 4K) due to plan-compilation overhead, only turning slightly favorable at 128K (37.90s vs 38.31s).
project_relevance: Falls in the serving/runtime/compiler direction: a serving-time IR and compiler-executor for plan-driven KV access, complementary to RAG serving cache-reuse work (RAGCache, CacheBlend, TurboRAG, RAGO) which targets prefill/scheduling/cache reuse rather than decode-time KV consumption. For our briefing it is a horizontal observation with measured but modest decode-throughput gains (1.08-1.19x) and a quality-preserving KV-reduction trajectory; deployability beyond Graph-RAG-style long-context QA is unproven.

evidence_gaps.question: What GPU hardware, batch size, and request concurrency were used for the vLLM/GraphSpec throughput (TPS) and TTFT measurements, since these materially determine the absolute and relative numbers?
Which LLM backbone(s) and parameter sizes were evaluated in the 4K-128K Tables 2-5, and is SPIQA the dataset for the full sweep (not only the 100-sample audit)?
